<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - Unity MCP is a two‐component, local “bridge” system that lets LLM-based MCP Clients (e.g. Claude Desktop, Cursor, VSCode Copilot) drive the Unity Editor.  
   - It consists of:  
     • UnityMcpBridge – a Unity Package (C#) loaded into the Editor (Editor + Runtime code)  
     • UnityMcpServer – a Python 3.12 microservice (uv-driven) that relays MCP calls  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level directories:  
     • UnityMcpBridge/ – contains the Unity Package, split into:  
       – Editor/ (Data, Helpers, Models, Tools, Windows, asmdef files)  
       – Runtime/ (Serialization converters, asmdef)  
     • UnityMcpServer/src/ – Python service, with server.py, port_discovery.py, config.py, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, plus a tools/ subpackage that mirrors the Bridge’s tool commands  
   - Other files: Dockerfile (server containerization), deploy-dev.bat & restore-dev.bat (deployment scripts)  

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Core flow diagram:  
     [Your LLM via MCP Client] ↔ [Unity MCP Server (Python)] ↔ [Unity MCP Bridge (Unity Editor)]  
   - Lists supported tools (manage_asset, manage_scene, manage_script, etc.) and setup steps (auto-configure vs manual)  
   - Emphasizes JSON-RPC over a local port, uv CLI invocation, and asmdef based plugin  

4. How to create the system design diagram  
   a. Main components to represent:  
      • External MCP Client (LLM tooling)  
      • UnityMcpServer (Python microservice)  
      • UnityMcpBridge (C# Unity Package) – subdivided into Editor module and Runtime module  
      • Unity Editor (hosting the Bridge and exposing UnityEditor APIs)  
   b. Relationships & interactions:  
      1. MCP Client uses uv CLI → starts/connects to Python server on discovered port (port_discovery.py).  
      2. Python server (server.py) listens for JSON requests, dispatches to src/tools/* handlers.  
      3. Bridge (Editor code) establishes a WebSocket/HTTP connection to Python server, receives JSON commands.  
      4. Bridge deserializes payload (Runtime.Serialization), invokes UnityEditor API via ToolRegistry and Helpers.  
      5. Results flow back through the same path to the MCP Client.  
   c. Architectural patterns & design principles:  
      - Plugin architecture in Unity with separate asmdef assemblies for Editor and Runtime  
      - Mirror pattern: each Python “tool” has a matching C# implementation  
      - Message-bus/JSON-RPC for decoupling Unity process from external tooling  
      - Local microservice pattern for ease of deployment and isolation  
   d. Key technologies, frameworks, and libraries:  
      - C# (.NET Standard) with UnityEditor and UnityEngine APIs  
      - Python 3.12 with uv (Astral.sh) for CLI orchestration  
      - pyproject.toml & uv.lock for Python packaging  
      - JSON for message serialization (MCP protocol)  

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram  
   - Emphasize component separation: front-end (MCP Client), service layer (Python server), plugin layer (Unity Bridge), and host (Unity Editor)  
   - For each layer, group related modules (e.g. Bridge.Editor/Tools, Bridge.Runtime/Serialization) as sub-boxes  
   - Highlight extensibility points (where new tools can be added) and configuration flows (auto-configure vs manual edits to MCP Client config file)  

6. Elements to include in the diagram  
   - Clear, descriptive box labels for each component and submodule  
   - Directional arrows showing request/response flows, annotated with protocols (JSON-RPC, WebSocket, uv CLI)  
   - Color coding or distinct shapes:  
     • Python server (green gears)  
     • Unity Bridge (blue cube)  
     • External client (yellow cloud or terminal)  
     • Unity Editor (gray application window)  

7. Detail to capture  
   - The Editor vs Runtime boundary within the Bridge package  
   - Port discovery and server startup flow (port_discovery.py → server.py)  
   - How “Auto-Configure” writes to the MCP Client’s config file vs Manual Configuration snippets  
   - The round-trip of commands: MCP Client → Python Server → Bridge → UnityEditor API → Bridge → Server → Client  

Use a layered diagram (top: MCP Client, middle: Python Server, bottom: Unity Bridge + Editor) with sub-layers for modules. Label every arrow, group related files under module boxes, and apply consistent color coding to distinguish languages and processes.
